items.abstract:
BACKGROUND

Differential diagnosis is an important skill, central to the clinical reasoning process. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in this task among other clinical reasoning tasks. However, study instruments have not replicated the likely use of LLMs in clinical environments and LLM performance has been defined subjectively.

 OBJECTIVE

The purpose of this paper was to assess LLM ability in generating a prioritized differential diagnosis by using objective benchmarks in response to a brief clinical vignette and comparing these benchmarks to experienced clinicians.

 METHODS

This cross-sectional study utilized a survey with three clinical vignettes of 50 words or less. As a convenience sampling strategy in this study, the study group included the most recent versions of commonly used LLMs as of the study period. Each LLM participant was prompted, “Provide a differential diagnosis for this patient’s [chief complaint]. List potential diagnoses without additional explanations.” Zero-shot prompting was used to evaluate each LLM, and two iterations were measured. Outcomes included top slot diagnosis, differential concordance index, list length, time to completion, word count, and number of citable references included. A reference panel of experienced emergency and internal medicine clinicians allowed for comparison in this skill.

 RESULTS

Ten different versions of LLMs were tested on each of the three vignettes. Top slot diagnosis concordance with the reference panel was 94.8% with eight of the ten LLM versions agreeing with the reference panel for 100% of the vignette iterations. Median list length per differential for LLMs (12, 10-15) was significantly greater than the reference panel lists (6, 5-9.5; X 5.95, p=0.000). LLM differential lists exhibited a variable concordance with reference panel lists with 20.1% of the lists containing unsupported items. LLMs provided differential lists in a significantly shorter amount of time as compared to the reference panel (X 4.99, p=0.001).

 CONCLUSIONS

Despite high top slot concordance with experienced clinician differential lists, LLM lists were significantly longer and exhibited variable global concordance which could lead to unnecessary testing and treatment. Future studies are needed to understand the implications of utilizing LLMs’ for diagnostic reasoning tasks in a clinical setting.
title: Measuring Benchmarks for Differential Diagnosis Performance in Large Language Models, A Cross-Sectional Comparative Cohort Analysis (Preprint)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced natural language processing in biomedical research, however, their reliance on implicit, statistical representations often results in factual inaccuracies or hallucinations, posing significant concerns in high-stakes biomedical contexts.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To overcome these limitations, we developed BTE-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that integrates the reasoning capabilities of advanced language models with explicit mechanistic evidence sourced from BioThings Explorer, an API federation of more than sixty authoritative biomedical knowledge sources. We systematically evaluated BTE-RAG in comparison to traditional LLM-only methods across three benchmark datasets that we created from DrugMechDB. These datasets specifically targeted gene-centric mechanisms (798 questions), metabolite effects (201 questions), and drug–biological process relationships (842 questions). On the gene-centric task, BTE-RAG increased accuracy from 51% to 75.8% for GPT-4o mini and from 69.8% to 78.6% for GPT-4o. In metabolite-focused questions, the proportion of responses with cosine similarity scores of at least 0.90 rose by 82% for GPT-4o mini and 77% for GPT-4o. While overall accuracy was consistent in the drug–biological process benchmark, the retrieval method enhanced response concordance, producing a greater than 10% increase in high-agreement answers (from 129 to 144) using GPT-4o.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Federated knowledge retrieval provides transparent improvements in accuracy for large language models, establishing BTE-RAG as a valuable and practical tool for mechanistic exploration and translational biomedical research.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
title: Federated Knowledge Retrieval Elevates Large Language Model Performance on Biomedical Benchmarks

items.abstract: <jats:p>This analysis critically examines the application of quantum mechanical concepts&mdash;such as entanglement, indistinguishability, and Bose Einstein statistics &mdash; to language and cognitive processes as proposed in the paper. While the interdisciplinary approach is creative, significant theoretical and empirical challenges arise when translating quantum principles to human cognition. Key issues include the contextual and qualitative nature of cognitive processes, which differ fundamentally from the predictable, probabilistic behaviors observed in quantum systems. Cognitive phenomena are shaped by factors like emotional state, social context, and personal memory, which have no direct analogy in quantum mechanics. The assumption that words or cognitive "particles" are indistinguishable, as quantum particles are, overlooks the unique and dynamic contextual dependencies in language. Moreover, empirical support for such quantum-cognitive parallels remains limited, and the paper&rsquo;s application of quantum statistics to word frequency distributions may reflect a coincidental pattern rather than a fundamental process. This assessment suggests that while the paper&rsquo;s quantum analogies could foster new interdisciplinary discussions, they risk speculative overreach if treated as foundational principles for understanding cognition. Effective interdisciplinary integration would require rigorous empirical validation within cognitive science, as well as caution against reductionist interpretations that might simplify the rich complexities of human thought. Future research may benefit from more context-sensitive and evidence-based models that align more closely with established cognitive theories, thereby maintaining the intellectual richness of both quantum mechanics and cognitive science without forcing an untested theoretical bridge between them.</jats:p>
title: Comment on the Paper Titled ’The Origin of Quantum Mechanical Statistics: Insights from Research on Human Language’ (arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.14924, 2024)
